step.title: Explore
step.question: Where could this life really work?
tagline: It is easy to fall in love with a place before checking whether your life can work there.
intro: Sometimes it works out. When it doesn't, the cost in time, money, and energy can be considerable.
Start with what you need, then look for a place that fits. Check what you can from home, using real information. Then visit and find out what it feels like to live there.
You finish with your Explore Summary: one or two places that fit your picture, what you know about them, what you still need to check, and what you want to test in real life.
Thinking of staying where you live now? This step is for you too. Use it to check whether your country and your region still fit your picture, instead of assuming they do.
Every exercise starts with a short explanation, then asks you to apply it to your own life.

what_you_need.title: What you need before you start
bullets: Your Working Direction from Step 1: what you want to explore next.
Your Life Picture and your must-haves and dealbreakers. They are your measuring stick in this step.
Your First Money Picture, which you will compare with real costs.
what_you_need.after: If you have not completed Step 1, you can still work through this step. Go back to Step 1 afterwards. In this step, you compare every place with the life you described in Step 1.

where_to_start.title: Where do you start?
where_to_start.intro: Use the descriptions below to choose your starting point.
rows: I have not chosen a country yet
You compare countries against what your life needs
I have chosen a country, but not a region
You compare regions inside that country
I have chosen a country and a region
You check that choice with real information
I am thinking of staying where I live now.
You check whether your own country and region still fit your picture, and compare them with one or two places that crossed your mind.
where_to_start.challenge: Before you skip Part 1 or Part 2, check what you already know. Have you visited in the cold, wet months, not just summer? Do you know the cost of living there, beyond a holiday budget? Have you checked your legal right to live there and the local rules for your plans: building, working, keeping animals, or running a business? If any answer is no, work through that part. A few hours now can save you years in the wrong place.

how_it_works.title: How this step works
bullets: Parts 1 and 2 are optional. Use them if you are still choosing a country or region. They are also useful if you are thinking of staying: they show whether the country and region where you live now still fit your picture best.
Parts 3, 4 and 5 are for everyone. They take you through research, a test visit, and your Explore Summary.
You do the research. I show you what to check and where to look. You find the answers for your own situation.

This step gives you an overview of what to check and where to look. A more detailed Portugal module is planned for later; it is not part of this course. It will cover land and building rules, fire safety, water, and local costs. Other planned modules will focus on finding and choosing land, buying a house, renovating an old house, living off-grid, Your Money Plan, and starting a company.
Three words come back again and again: known, estimate, unknown. Writing "unknown" is progress. It shows you what to find out next.
Each part ends with "What does this tell me?" Use your answers to complete a summary.
The people in the examples are made up. They show what an answer can look like. Your answers can be completely different.

word_help.title: Word help
items: something your new life really needs.
something you will not accept, even if everything else is good.
the two or three places you want to explore further.
the quiet, often cold or wet time of year.
official permission to live in a country for an extended period.
income you have evidence will continue in your new situation.

tips: Give Part 3 more than one evening. Spread it over a few weeks. Even ten minutes a day will help you make progress.

route.title: Your route through Step 2
rows: Write down what you are looking for

parts.label: Start
parts.title: What I am looking for
parts.promise: Before you look at any place, write down what you are measuring it against.
parts.intro_title: Why the measuring stick comes first
intro: Once you start looking at places, it is easy to let them change what you said you needed. Photographs show them at their best. Advertised prices do not include every cost. A visit in June tells you little about life there in February.
Write down what you need before you start looking. Then compare every place against the same list. You will then notice if you start changing your requirements because you prefer a certain place.
This page takes twenty minutes, and you use it in every part that follows.
parts.route_title: Write down what you are looking for
parts.talk: If you are moving with someone, each of you should complete this page separately. Then compare and talk about where your answers differ. Have that conversation now, before you arrive.

finish.title: What I Am Looking For
finish.description: The measuring stick you use for every place in this step.

fields.label: Bring your direction with you
fields.hint: Copy the most important lines from your Step 1 Working Direction.

fields.label: My life picture in three sentences
The direction(s) I want to explore
My must-haves: what this life needs
My dealbreakers: what I will not accept
What I am willing to invest: time, money, comfort
What kind of place does this life need?
fields.hint: Do not name a country yet. Describe the place your picture needs. Tick what is true for you.

options: A workshop or space to build

fields.hint: Now write the three things that matter most, in your own words. If a place cannot give you these three, it is not your place.

example.text: What matters most: (1) I can grow food at least eight months a year, (2) a hospital within 45 minutes because of my daughter, (3) internet good enough for video calls, because my income comes from clients abroad. Nice but not essential: near the sea.

parts.result: What I Am Looking For — the measuring stick you use for every place in this step.

parts.label: Part 1
parts.title: Which country?
parts.promise: Ten honest questions that separate a place you like in theory from a place where your life can work.
parts.can_skip: If you have chosen your country and answered the friendly challenge under "Where do you start?", go to Part 2. You can return here if your research in Part 3 uncovers a barrier, such as not being allowed to live there.
parts.intro_title: Start with the list, not the map
intro: When I chose a country, I began with a list of what my life needed. Then I checked which countries fitted. It sounds obvious, but it is easy to start with somewhere you already like and try to make it work.
A list gives you something to score, compare and check. Your feeling about a country matters too, and you will explore that in Part 4. This part helps you decide which places are worth visiting.
The ten factors below give you a starting point. I used the first eight myself and added the last two later, because I have seen how often they stop a plan.

finish.title: My Country Choice
finish.description: One country to explore, with your reasons and your open questions.

exercises.title: The ten factors

rows: Look at the whole year. How hot, cold, wet or dry does it get? Is there enough water? How do you cope with that climate?
Land, space, a workshop, clients, a job, a school, a studio, quiet. What does your picture from Step 1 physically need?
What are you allowed to do there? Build, renovate, work from home, keep animals, live off-grid, run a business, work as a foreigner.
4. Support and costs from the state

Some countries offer support for newcomers or particular plans; others make the process expensive or slow. Taxes and support change, so check any figure you find on a forum against an official source.
Can you connect with people? People doing something similar? How hard is the local language for you, and how much will you need it?
Distance to a doctor, hospital, pharmacy, shops, and schools. What does healthcare cost, and who is allowed to use it?
What can you afford to buy or rent, and what will daily life cost? A place that fits your budget gives you more time to settle in.
Roads, electricity, water, internet, public transport, deliveries. Can you actually work and live there?
9. Your legal right to live there
Can you get permission to stay? What do you have to prove: income, savings, insurance, work? How long does it take?
10. Distance to the people you love
Flights, cost, travel time. And a harder question: if someone close to you becomes ill, how quickly could you reach them?

tips: Factors 3, 4, 6 and 9 involve rules that change. Use official government sources, record the date you checked, and check again before deciding. Part 3 shows you how.

exercises.title: Score your countries
intro: Scoring helps you see your reasons clearly. It shows which countries fall short on something important and where you still need information. The highest total is not necessarily the right choice.

start_here.prompt: Choose two to four countries you are curious about. Thinking of staying? Include your own country. Score each factor: 2 = good for me, 1 = maybe, 0 = no. Leave a box empty if you do not know yet, and add it to your research list.

row_labels: 4. Support and costs from the state

exercises.challenge: Look at the zeros before the total. A zero on a must-have rules a country out, no matter how high it scores elsewhere. Then look at the empty boxes: those tell you what to research next.

story.text: As Bali became busier, I missed working with my hands and growing things. A YouTube channel about self-sufficient living helped me see what I wanted next. I listed what that life needed: climate and soil, water, rules for land and off-grid living, community, healthcare nearby, an affordable place to live, and the infrastructure to stay connected. I compared five countries: Portugal, New Zealand, Costa Rica, Australia and Canada. Portugal fitted best.

exercises.title: The two questions that end most plans
intro: Two questions can stop an otherwise appealing plan. They are easy to leave until the end, but they need answers early.

Am I allowed to live there? Every country sets its own conditions for who can stay and for how long. Your passport, income, work and family situation all matter. Someone else's experience doesn't determine what applies to you.

Can I afford to live there? Compare the cost of an ordinary month with your First Money Picture from Step 1. Include housing, food, energy, healthcare, transport, insurance, and something for enjoyment. A holiday budget will not answer this question.

start_here.prompt: Write what you know about your situation today. Use "unknown" where you still need an answer. It gives you something clear to investigate.

fields.label: Am I allowed to live there? What I know today
What I would have to prove
Can I afford a normal month there? What I know today
What I still need to find out, and where

where_to_check: Rules about living in a country come from that country's government, not from a blog or me. For Portugal, the official pages are gov.pt (theme: foreigners in Portugal), aima.gov.pt (residence), and vistos.mne.gov.pt (visas). Other countries have similar official pages. Write the date you checked next to every answer.
exercises.expert_work: Take questions about tax, residence law, pensions and investments to a qualified adviser in the country concerned. The answers depend on your circumstances. Use this workbook to prepare the questions you need to ask.

go_deeper.prompt: Take your best country and argue against it for ten minutes. What is the strongest reason not to go there? Write it down. If you cannot find one, you have not looked hard enough yet.

summary.title: What does this tell me?
summary.intro: Read through your answers, then use these questions to complete the summary below:
questions: Which country fits most of my ten factors?
Where are my zeros, and are they on a must-have?
What do I still not know, and where can I find it?
summary.prompt: Now bring it together in My Country Choice. Short sentences are enough.

fields.label: The country I want to explore further
Two or three reasons why
Countries I let go of, and why
My biggest doubt about this country
What I must check before I decide, and where

example.text: Country: Portugal. Why: I feel well in that climate, my money goes further than at home, and I work online, so I need reliable internet. I ruled out Costa Rica because it is too far from my parents and flights are expensive. My biggest doubt is winter in a stone house. I need to find out how people heat their homes and what it costs.

summary.result: My Country Choice — one country to explore, with your reasons and your open questions.

parts.staying: Do this part anyway, with your own country in it. Score it like any other, next to one or two countries that have crossed your mind. If your own country still comes out best, you have checked it instead of assuming it. That is a strong reason to stay.

parts.label: Part 2
parts.title: Which region?
parts.promise: A country is not one place. Inside one country, life can be completely different from one valley to the next.
parts.can_skip: If you have chosen a region and answered the friendly challenge under "Where do you start?", go to Part 3. Read the ten region questions first, though. It takes two minutes and can bring up something you haven't considered.
parts.intro_title: The region decides your daily life
intro: Once you have chosen a country, it is tempting to visit the best-known region and buy there. Take time to compare it with other areas before spending money.
Your country decides your paperwork. Your region shapes your daily life: the weather, neighbours, costs, the journey to the hospital, internet, and how busy or quiet it is in August and January.

Keep two or three regions on your list long enough to compare them properly. A second visit elsewhere helps you notice what you missed the first time. By the third, you will have a clearer sense of what matters to you.
parts.talk: Find two or three people who actually live in the regions on your list, in online groups or through people you know. Ask them one question: "What do you wish you had known before you moved here?" The answer is usually not in any brochure.

finish.title: My Region Shortlist
finish.description: Two or three regions, with what you like and what worries you.

rows: Summer heat, winter cold, rain, wind, fog, snow. In one country you can find all of them.
Flat land or mountains, forest or open ground, soil, water, and the risk of fire or flooding.
Houses, land, rent. Within one country, prices can differ by three or four times.
How far is it to a doctor, a hospital, a pharmacy? How long does an ambulance take?
Shops, schools, sports, banks, post offices, fuel. How far would you travel for everyday needs?
Jobs, clients, tourists, seasons. Or can you bring your income with you?
Airport, train, motorway. How easy is it for you to leave, and for people to visit?
Check the speed at a specific address on an ordinary evening, rather than simply asking whether internet is available.
Who lives there? Are there other newcomers? How much of the local language will you need?
Some places are packed in summer and empty in winter. Would both seasons suit you?

exercises.title: Portugal: the map in simple words
intro: This section focuses on Portugal. If you are considering another country, use the same questions to understand its regions.

Mainland Portugal is divided into 18 districts, plus the two island regions, Madeira and the Azores. For statistics, the mainland is often grouped into five regions: North, Centre, Lisbon area, Alentejo and Algarve.

The weather is not the same everywhere, and the differences are bigger than most people expect for a small country. The national weather institute, IPMA, classifies the climate of the mainland like this:

rows: Inland Douro valley (part of Bragança district) and most areas south of the Montejunto–Estrela mountain line
Almost all areas north of that mountain line, plus the west coast of Alentejo and the Algarve
A small area in the Beja district, in the Alentejo
Eastern islands: mild, dry summers (Csb). Central and western islands: ocean climate, wetter all year (Cfb)

tables.lead: Beyond the weather: what else changes from region to region. Weather is often the first difference you notice. These four areas also vary between municipalities and can surprise newcomers. For now, know which questions to ask. A more detailed Portugal module, planned for later, will cover each one.
rows: Every municipality has its own plan, the PDM (Plano Diretor Municipal), that says what may be built where. Land is usually classed as rústico (rural) or urbano (urban). On rural land, building a new house is often not allowed. These rules have changed recently, so check the current situation for the exact plot before you fall for it.
Large parts of the interior have a high fire risk. Owners must keep the land around houses clear of vegetation, and this is checked. Ask what it means for the place you look at, in work and in cost.
Mains water does not reach everywhere. In the countryside, many homes use a well or a borehole, and these may need permission or registration with the environment agency.

Lisbon, Porto, the coast and the Algarve cost much more than the interior. The interior is cheaper, and programmes sometimes support people who move there. Those programmes change, so check what is current.

where_to_check: IPMA, Climate normals and climate classification, ipma.pt (checked 20 September 2026). IPMA also publishes average temperature and rainfall per month for weather stations across the country, for the periods 1971–2000, 1981–2010 and 1991–2020. Look up the station closest to the place you are considering, and look at the winter months, not only the summer ones.

Building and land-use rules are set locally. Start with the town or municipal council where the place is: its website, or its planning office. Most countries also have a national website that publishes the local plans. Ask the council, or a local fire service or forestry office, whether there is a fire risk and whether owners have to clear land. For water, find out whether mains water reaches the address. If it doesn't, check whether a well or borehole needs a permit, and who issues it; this is usually the national or regional environment agency. Write down the source and the date you checked. In Portugal: the câmara municipal and pcgt.dgterritorio.gov.pt (land use), sgifr.gov.pt (fire safety) and apambiente.pt (wells and boreholes). Checked 27 September 2026.
tips: Inland and higher up means hotter summers and colder winters. Near the ocean means milder, but also windier and damper. Many older houses here were built for summer heat rather than winter cold, so before you fall in love with a house, find out how it works in every season: how it is heated in winter, and how it stays cool in summer.

start_here.prompt: Choose two to four regions. Thinking of staying? Include the region where you live now. Score each factor: 2 = good for me, 1 = maybe, 0 = no. Leave a box empty if you do not know yet, and add it to your research list.

story.text: I live near the Serra da Estrela mountains, in the district of Guarda. Coming from Bali, I didn't want a tropical climate. I wanted real seasons, but not a Northern European climate either. That brought me to central Portugal: far enough from the sea to avoid the wind, with mountains nearby, more rain, and summers less hot than, for example, in the Alentejo. There is also room to grow food. When I was searching, my budget was at most €100,000 for 2 to 3 hectares. Climate mattered just as much as price, so I looked mainly around Viseu, Guarda and Setúbal. In the end, central Portugal fitted best. Your list will depend on your own needs. Keeping two or three regions open long enough to compare them helped me choose.

example.text: Region 1 scores well on price and nature, but the hospital is 50 minutes away. Region 2 costs more and has everything nearby. I am keeping both for now. On my test visit, I will find out how that drive feels in winter rain, rather than judging it on a sunny day in June.

summary.intro: Read through your answers, then use these questions to complete the summary below:
questions: Which two or three regions stay on my list?
What makes them different from each other?
What would make me drop one of them?
summary.prompt: Now bring it together in My Region Shortlist. Short sentences are enough.

fields.label: My shortlist: two or three regions
What attracts me in each one
What worries me in each one
Regions I let go, and why
What I must find out about each (Part 3)

summary.result: My Region Shortlist — two or three regions, with what you like and what worries you.

parts.staying: Is the region where you live now still the best place for your picture? Score it as Region 1, next to one or two other regions in your own country. Sometimes the change you need isn't a new country, but a move of an hour: closer to nature, family, or work you enjoy.

parts.label: Part 3
parts.title: Check it from home
parts.promise: You can find out a great deal about a place before booking a ticket.
parts.intro_title: Research is a skill, and it has rules
intro: Research takes patience. It also helps you spot expensive problems before you commit to a place.

Build a profile for each place on your shortlist using sources you can check. Memories, forum posts and conversations can raise useful questions, but they are not enough on their own. Follow these three rules.

Write the source and the date. Prices and rules change, so a fact without a date may already be out of date. Keep a record so you can see where an answer came from and check whether it is still current.

Mark how sure you are. Known means you have checked an official or reliable source. Estimate means your best figure or judgement, still to be confirmed. Unknown means you do not have an answer yet. Naming an unknown gives you a clear question to investigate.
Separate rules from experiences. A government page tells you what is allowed. A person who lives there tells you what it is like. You need both, and they answer different questions.

finish.title: My Place Profiles
finish.description: Real information for each place, with your unknowns written down honestly.

exercises.title: The money check
intro: Compare your First Money Picture from Step 1 with what life costs in this place. You are checking how close your first figures were, where the gaps are, and what remains unknown.

start_here.prompt: Use your First Money Picture to compare your estimates with the costs you find for an ordinary month in this place.

fields.hint: Now check whether your income will continue in this place. Moving can affect remote work, clients, a pension or a job in different ways. As in Step 1, count confirmed and agreed income. Hoped income stays out.

story.text: Here is what an ordinary month near the Serra da Estrela costs me in 2026. Energy costs about €200 a month before installing a solar system. Fast fibre internet is €20, and health insurance is €60. Food costs €400 to €500, including a meal out once a week. Fuel is about €150. These figures don't cover all my monthly costs, or what I invested in renovating the house.

where_to_check: Do not use "cost of living" websites as your only source. Look at real prices: property and rental websites for that exact area, supermarket websites, energy company price pages, and insurance quotes for your own situation. For general statistics in Portugal, you can use INE, ine.pt (the national statistics institute), and pordata.pt. Write the date next to everything.
exercises.challenge: Compare this total with your Step 1 estimate. If they differ by more than 20%, go back through both sets of figures. Find out what accounts for the difference before you go further.

exercises.title: The legal check
intro: You are checking one thing: are you allowed to live there, and what do you have to prove? The answer depends on your passport, your income and your family situation, so write down what applies to you, not what applies in general.

row_labels: Which route applies to my passport?
What must I prove: income, savings, insurance, work, a place to live?
Where and when do I apply: before I travel, or after I arrive?
How long does it take, and what does it cost?
What does it mean for my family members?
What do I have to do every year to keep it?

tables.lead: For Portugal, the official information below covers two different routes. Start with the one that applies to your passport:
rows: If you hold an EU, EEA, Andorran or Swiss passport

You can enter and stay without a visa. If you stay longer than three months, request a registration certificate at the câmara municipal (town hall) in the area where you live. The official page says you must do this within 30 days after those first three months, and that you bring a valid ID or passport plus a declaration about your situation: that you work there, that you have enough means and health cover, or that you are studying. Source: aima.gov.pt, checked 20 September 2026.
If you hold any other passport

You normally need a visa before you travel, from a Portuguese consulate. The official visa portal divides long-stay visas into temporary stay visas (for stays under one year) and residency visas (valid for four months and giving two entries, during which you apply for your residence permit with AIMA), plus a separate visa for skilled job seekers. Which one fits you depends on your purpose: work, remote work, study, income from outside, family. Source: vistos.mne.gov.pt, checked 20 September 2026.

tips: Rules like these change, and details matter more than summaries. Treat the two paragraphs above as a map, not as advice: open the official pages yourself, for your own situation, and write down the date. If your case is not simple, pay a lawyer for one hour. It is the cheapest hour you will spend.

exercises.title: The daily life check
intro: Now look at everyday life. You can answer many of these questions from home with a map, official websites, and a few messages.

Look at time too. A place can give you more say over your time, but it can also bring new must-dos: land to clear, a house to maintain, paperwork, longer drives to shops and doctors. More land does not automatically mean more freedom.

start_here.prompt: Answer for each place on your shortlist.

row_labels: Distance and time to a hospital
Family doctor: is there one taking new patients?
How healthcare works for someone like me
Schools, and the language they teach in
Internet speed at a real address there
Nearest airport and travel time home
Winter: how cold, how wet, how long
Summer: how hot, how dry, fire risk
Water: where does it come from?
How much local language will I need?
What may be built or changed there (municipal plan)
Fire risk and the land clearing required
New must-dos this place would bring (land, house, paperwork, travel)

story.text: My own daily life check, today: 15 minutes to the local hospital, and 40 minutes to a larger one in Viseu or Guarda. Fast fibre internet at my address. Water from a well on my own land. Most of my electricity now comes from solar panels.

where_to_check: In Portugal, the public health service is the SNS (sns.gov.pt). Official service pages for people coming from abroad, including health, tax and social security numbers, are on gov.pt under the theme "Estrangeiros em Portugal" (foreigners in Portugal). Checked on 20 September 2026.
tips: A more detailed Portugal module is planned for later; it is not part of this course. It will cover land, building rules, fire safety and water, with official sources and dates.

example.text: Hospital: 35 minutes by car, and I checked the map for winter road conditions, not summer. Family doctor: unknown; I will ask when I visit. Internet: the provider says 100 Mbit at that address, but a neighbour in the village told me it drops in the evening. So: estimate, not known.

exercises.title: Talk to people who live there
intro: People who live there can tell you things the numbers cannot. Their answers also reflect their own circumstances, so choose whom you ask and make your questions specific.

A recent arrival may still be caught up in the excitement of moving. Someone who has had a bad experience may see the place through that experience. Listen to both, and talk to at least three residents, including someone who has lived there for years.

start_here.prompt: Find three people who live in the area, not just people who have visited. Ask the questions below, especially the last one.
bullets: What does a normal Tuesday in February look like here?
What did you underestimate before you came?
What do you pay, roughly, for energy in winter?
How long did the paperwork take, and what went wrong?
If you had to do it again, what would you do differently?

questions: Which place still meets my must-haves after this research?
Where did reality differ from my guess?

parts.label: Part 4
parts.title: Test it in real life
parts.promise: Research tells you a lot. A visit shows you how it feels to be there.
parts.intro_title: Go as a tester, not as a tourist
intro: Visit with your future daily life in mind.

A holiday in good weather, with a central hotel and meals out, can leave you loving a place without knowing how ordinary life would feel there. Plan this visit around the questions a holiday cannot answer.

Visit outside the high season if you can. February rain tells you something different from a sunny afternoon. Decide what the trip must answer before you book, and make time for ordinary things: grocery shopping, a doctor's waiting room, a school, a Sunday when shops are closed. Keep those questions in mind even when the weather and a good lunch make the place feel perfect.
I would also visit twice. You notice things the second time that you missed the first time.
parts.talk: Did you travel with someone? Do this exercise separately first, then read your answers to each other. If you travelled alone, send your three answers to someone who knows you well and ask what they hear.

finish.title: My Test Visit Report
finish.description: What you learned in person, written down while it is fresh.

How long I stay
Places on my list
How I travel there and around
Where I stay, and why it suits the test better than a hotel in the centre
My budget for this trip
The three questions this trip must answer

exercises.challenge: Write your three questions before you book anything, and give this page to someone who knows you. Ask them to hold you to it when you come back excited.

exercises.title: The real-life checklist
intro: Take this with you. Tick what you actually did, not what you planned to do.

options: Checked the drive to the airport
Priced a real house or rental

fields.hint: Write your notes the same evening. After a few days, memories blur, especially the differences between places.

story.text: In April and May 2024, I spent two months travelling through Portugal in a campervan. The trip cost about €4,000. I visited plots I had shortlisted and could stop wherever I wanted. I was surprised by how connected I felt to one region and how little I felt in another. No amount of reading could have told me that. Buying was not the plan for the trip. I visited 25 plots, with prices from about €30,000 to €200,000. Location, any area classified as urban (building) land, and existing buildings all affected the price. I eventually bought the third plot: 2.5 hectares. I felt at home on the land and in the surrounding area, and kept thinking about it as I visited the others. On a second visit, I met the owners. They showed me things I had missed the first time. I signed a promissory contract in August 2024 and the deed at the notary in November. With a good lawyer, it went smoothly, and registering the sale took only about a month after that. Having already made my financial plan from Step 1, I felt comfortable committing when the opportunity came.

tips: I took two lessons from that trip. Visit a place twice before deciding: you notice more the second time. And compare several places. Seeing the other plots helped me understand why the third one felt right.

exercises.title: The honest evening question
intro: On your last evening, find somewhere quiet and answer these three questions before discussing the trip with anyone else. Give yourself time to form your own view.

fields.label: Could I live an ordinary week here, with laundry, work, bad weather and nothing special happening?
What did I notice that I would rather have overlooked?
What surprised me in a good way?

example.text: Could I live an ordinary week here? Yes, but not in the village I loved most. It is beautiful, yet after three days I had spoken to nobody. I felt more at ease in the small town 20 minutes away. It was not on my list, and it may be the most useful thing I learned.

questions: Did the place answer my three questions?

What do I still need to see or test?

fields.label: Where I went, and when

parts.label: Part 5
parts.title: Bring it together
parts.promise: One place. One honest picture of it. And the decision about what comes next.
parts.intro_title: What this step can and cannot decide
intro: Bring your research and visit notes together so you and the people close to you can see the whole picture.

Your Explore Summary identifies a place worth planning for and the questions you still need to answer. You make the decision itself in Step 3, where you check the plan, the money and the timing together.

Expect some gaps in the summary. A few weeks of research will not answer everything. If you have no unknowns left, ask yourself honestly whether you stopped asking difficult questions once you started to like the place.
parts.talk: Share your Explore Summary with the people affected by this decision. Explain what you are considering and listen to their concerns while you still have time to work through them.

finish.title: My Explore Summary
finish.description: One place, one honest picture, and your decision about what comes next.

exercises.choice_explanations_intro: All four answers are good ones:
choice_explanations: Go further with this place. Step 3 turns it into a real plan, with money, timing and paperwork.
Keep two places open. Take both into Step 3 and compare what it would take to make each one work.
Look somewhere else. It is better to change direction now than after signing a contract. Return to Part 1 or 2 with what you have learned.
Stay and build the life you want here. Staying is a real result. It takes the same work: deciding, planning, and building. See "If you decide to stay" below.

exercises.title: Update your money picture

start_here.prompt: Return to your First Money Picture from Step 1 and replace estimates with the figures you have checked. Then make a separate check: with these costs, how many months could you live there without income?

exercises.expert_work: Before you move money between countries, sell a house, or change where you pay tax, speak to a qualified adviser in both countries. This workbook helps you arrive with the right questions. It never gives the answers.

exercises.title: If you decide to stay
intro: You may discover that the life you want does not require another country. If you scored where you live now in Part 1 or Part 2 and it came out best, you have checked that, not assumed it. Staying is a real result. Your answers usually point to one of four things:
intro_bullets: What I want is here, but my life needs to be organised differently. Focus on time, work, home and people.
What I want is somewhere else, but the time is not right. Look at what needs to change in money, family, work or health. Write down what must be in place before you go, and by when.
I wanted a change more than a different place. Use your Life Picture from Step 1 to choose one concrete change for the next three months.
What I want is in my own country, but in another region. Take your region shortlist from Part 2 into Step 3, and plan it like any other move: the money, the timing and the people involved.

fields.label: What I now know I really want
What I will change in the next three months
What staying protects, and what it costs me
What must be true before I look abroad again?
When I will look at this again

tips: Put a review date in your calendar today. A decision to wait is only a decision if it has a date.

parts.result: My Explore Summary — one place, one honest picture, and your decision about what comes next.

closing.title: What comes next
closing.intro: This step takes patience. You now know more about the place than photographs can show, and you have a clearer list of what still needs checking.
bullets: Going further with a place? Step 3, Decide, turns it into a plan: the money, the timing, the paperwork and the order of things.
Keeping two places open? Take both into Step 3. A plan on paper is the cheapest way to compare them.
Staying for now? Use "If you decide to stay" and put a review date in your calendar.
tips: Keep your Explore Summary somewhere easy to find. In a year, you can look back at what you expected and see what turned out to be true.
final: A place does not become yours because it is beautiful.
It becomes yours because your life can work there.
